newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania able to pay its crude imports - officials.
newsitem.headline: Romania able to pay its crude imports - officials.

text.p: Senior officials in the oil sector have denied suggestions that Romania is uncreditworthy for oil imports and pledged to proceed with vital monthly purchases of 700,000 tonnes during the coming winter.
Disruptions to supplies of crude, following a legal dispute embroiling the country's national oil company, have caused huge queues at petrol pumps throughought Romania.
Vifor Ionita, Vice-President of the National Oil Company (CRP), told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday that predictions of imminent shutdowns of Romania's 12 refineries would not come true.
"It's true we have to make great efforts to pay for the imported crude oil," Ionita said. "We will pay for every drop of crude we bring in."
Media reports said the CRP was unable to pay for hundreds of thousands of tonnes of crude oil already discharged at the main oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Constanta.

An official with Petrolexportimport SA, the country's main oil trader, said his company had made arrangements with the state Bancorex SA bank on Tuesday to issue letters of guarantee for some 500,000 tonnes of crude stored at Constanta.

"We are also arranging letters of guarantee for more than 200,000 tonnes of crude expected to arrive next week," said the official, who asked not to be identified. "We will import a minimum of 700,000 tonnes of crude in December. We already have nominated the tankers for more than half of that quantity."
A CRP source said crude from Constanta would be pumped to refineries early on Wednesday. Four big refineries hit by the shortage would resume "normal" activity this week, he added.

Motorists in provincial towns have spent hours waiting for fuel in recent days and prices almost doubled at some private stations. In Bucharest, queues were shorter as supplies have tended to be more reliable.
Oil industry sources say Romania has 25,000 tonnes of petrol and 16,000 tonnes of diesel oil in stock at refineries.
Ionita said the CRP's payment difficulties were mainly related to a halt in its talks with Chase Manhattan Corp on a $200 million revolving credit for crude imports.
An acute shortage of hard currency on the interbank market added to the problem, he said.
Talks bogged down after a court ruling ordering the suspension of a government decree creating the CRP last July.
"The halt to the talks has created credibility problems with some of our suppliers and their banks," Ionita said.
Court action to suspend the CRP was launched by a local private firm, General Trading and Investments Co SA (GTI), which accused the state-run holding of monopolistic practices.
The CRP has repeatedly denied GTI's charges and threatened to sue the company for libel and damages. Chase Manhattan asked the CRP to clarify its legal status.
Ionita said he hoped a memorandum signed with the bank on Monday would lead to new talks on the $200 million credit regardless of what was happening in the courts.
Chase Manhattan officials were unavailable for comment.
"I want to make it clear that for the time being there is no alternative to the CRP and everyone should stop and think that winter is coming," Ionita said.
